paper.title: Eureka: Human-Level Reward Design via Coding Large Language Models
paper.source_version: arXiv v2, 2024-04-30; latest public arXiv version verified 2026-08-30. Published at ICLR 2024, OpenReview IEduRUO55F. Official code evidence pinned to commit 9eee42808b52d8abc14845d1547bfde886403ccc (2024-05-03).

decision_relevance.why_admitted: Eureka is direct evidence for searching executable task-reward code while the world model and PPO trainer remain fixed, using policy fitness and component-level learning traces as feedback; it also tests human reward initialization and textual steering.
not_evidence_for: reference-dataset composition, mode discovery, state-machine synthesis, or closed-loop oracle design
safe or sandboxed execution of generated reward code
reward-only causality for the pen-spinning curriculum, which changes initialization and target schedule
generalization across controllers, optimizers, simulators, observation contracts, or training budgets
an untouched holdout metric, because task fitness F is used for both search and reporting
broad safety or alignment from the single 20-person Humanoid preference study
macOS or Apple-MPS compatibility of the NVIDIA Isaac Gym release

mechanisms.name: Fixed-world reward-design contract
mechanisms.description: The reward design problem separates world model M=(S,A,T), learning algorithm A_M, candidate reward R, resulting policy, and scalar policy fitness F; the search objective is to maximize F(A_M(R)).

mechanisms.name: Environment-as-context reward synthesis
mechanisms.description: A coding LLM receives a task description and environment snippets exposing state/action variables, then emits TorchScript-compatible Python returning total reward and a dictionary of named components.

mechanisms.name: In-context evolutionary reward search
mechanisms.description: Each iteration samples K independent reward programs, trains a policy for each executable program, ranks candidates by task fitness, mutates the best previous candidate using reflection, and preserves the best-so-far reward across iterations and random restarts.

mechanisms.name: Component-level reward reflection
mechanisms.description: The feedback prompt summarizes trajectories and max/mean/min values for named reward components and task fitness, allowing the LLM to change scales, functional forms, or components rather than relying on a scalar score alone.

mechanisms.name: One-step reward history
mechanisms.description: To fit the LLM context, the iterative prompt retains the initial system prompt plus only the most recent reward and reflection; earlier mutations are not preserved in the active dialogue.

mechanisms.name: Human reward initialization
mechanisms.description: A human-written reward can replace the first generated candidate, after which policy feedback and the standard mutation loop search for an improved reward.

mechanisms.name: Textual human steering
mechanisms.description: For the Humanoid study, one reward is sampled per iteration and colloquial human text replaces automatic reflection, steering subsequent reward code without model updating or direct low-level policy commands.

mechanisms.name: Generated-code training loop
mechanisms.description: The pinned release extracts an LLM code block, injects the function into an Isaac Gym task module, launches PPO as a subprocess, parses TensorBoard metrics and tracebacks, and selects the highest task score.

failure_modes.name: Invalid or suboptimal first-attempt code
failure_modes.description: A generated reward may fail to execute or may optimize poorly. Sixteen-sample batches contained an executable candidate in the tested environments, but this is an empirical observation, not a validity guarantee.

failure_modes.name: Single-run search noise
failure_modes.description: Intermediate candidates are ranked after one PPO run, whereas five runs are used only for the final reward; stochastic training can therefore change which reward is selected for mutation.

failure_modes.name: Fitness-function specification burden
failure_modes.description: Automated search requires a human-definable task fitness F. Behaviors such as stable or natural gait can be difficult to specify, and optimizing F may not align with human intent.

failure_modes.name: Trainer-dependent reward quality
failure_modes.description: Reward effectiveness depends on optimizer and hyperparameters. The benchmark held PPO fixed, and Eureka Dexterity curves were less smooth under hyperparameters tuned for human rewards.

failure_modes.name: Search/evaluation metric reuse
failure_modes.description: Fitness F is separate from the generated reward but selects candidates and reports final performance. The study does not provide an untouched holdout objective resistant to overfitting F.

failure_modes.name: Clipped aggregate and checkpoint maximum
failure_modes.description: The 52% headline clips each task's normalized score to [0,3], and the main comparison averages maxima over ten checkpoints; both choices must be preserved when interpreting the aggregate.

failure_modes.name: Policy-training search cost
failure_modes.description: Reward search nests many policy trainings. The reported system used eight A100 GPUs, up to sixteen candidates at once, and less than one day per run on that station.

failure_modes.name: Narrow human-steering evidence
failure_modes.description: Human steering is evaluated on one simulated Humanoid pair with twenty student raters; the preferred behavior is slower, and the result is not a broad safety evaluation.

failure_modes.name: Simulator and real-world scope
failure_modes.description: Most evidence uses one simulator and one RL algorithm; the paper lists a single MuJoCo Humanoid exception and only preliminary sim-to-real evidence.

failure_modes.name: Unsandboxed generated-code execution
failure_modes.description: The official release writes generated Python into an environment module and launches it in PPO subprocesses; the release provides no sandbox, side-effect proof, or safe reward DSL.

failure_modes.name: Release default mismatch
failure_modes.description: At the same pinned commit, README text says 5 iterations and 16 samples are defaults, while config.yaml sets 1 and 3. Reproduction requires an explicit resolved configuration.

failure_modes.name: NVIDIA/Linux release dependency
failure_modes.description: The release was tested on Ubuntu 20.04/22.04 with Isaac Gym Preview 4; it provides no evidence for native macOS or Apple-MPS execution.

evaluation.name: Fixed-PPO 29-task comparison
evaluation.description: Across nine Isaac and twenty Dexterity tasks, all final rewards use the same PPO implementation and task hyperparameters; Eureka is reported at or above human rewards on 83% of tasks with a clipped average normalized improvement of 52%.

evaluation.name: Evolution versus 32 first-attempt samples
evaluation.description: At an equal 32-candidate budget, two evolutionary iterations outperform drawing all candidates in the initial iteration on both benchmark suites.

evaluation.name: Component-reflection ablation
evaluation.description: Removing component-level reward reflection and retaining fitness snapshots reduces average normalized score by 28.6% over Isaac tasks, with larger reported deterioration on higher-dimensional tasks.

evaluation.name: Humanoid text-steering preference study
evaluation.description: Fifteen of twenty users prefer the text-reflection behavior to baseline Eureka, while its forward velocity is 5.58 versus 7.53; this is one pairwise simulated behavior comparison.

evaluation.name: Pen-spinning curriculum
evaluation.description: The same learned reward is used first for random pen reorientation and then to fine-tune a pretrained policy on a waypoint sequence; scratch and pretrained-only variants do not complete one cycle, so the result is not reward-only evidence.

evaluation.name: Dexterity aggregate uncertainty
evaluation.description: Mean, median, interquartile mean, and probability-of-improvement analyses use 100 runs with 95% confidence intervals across twenty Dexterity tasks.

evaluation.name: Paper/release identity audit
evaluation.description: The paper's 5-iteration, 16-sample search differs from config.yaml defaults of 1 and 3, and the README advertises the paper-scale values as defaults; exact reproduction requires a pinned override manifest.

evidence.locator: Header and abstract; arXiv v2 dated 30 April 2024
evidence.claim: The exact analyzed public paper is arXiv 2310.12931v2 with the listed title and nine authors.
The formal reward-design problem separates world model M, learning algorithm A_M, reward R, policy and policy fitness F, with objective F(A_M(R)).
Eureka uses environment code and task text to sample executable reward programs, evaluate them by fitness, reflect on the best, and update the best-so-far reward.
The experiments use five independent runs, five search iterations and sixteen samples per iteration; the next iteration conditions on the prior best reward and its reflection.
Reward reflection tracks component and fitness values through policy training and is intended to provide credit assignment that depends on the chosen RL algorithm.
The generated reward must be TorchScript-compatible Python returning total reward plus a component dictionary and using only exposed environment attributes.
The benchmark uses gpt-4-0314, 29 tasks and 10 morphologies; final rewards share a fixed PPO implementation and task hyperparameters, use five runs, and report maxima over ten checkpoints.
The paper reports at-or-above-human reward performance on 83% of tasks, evolution and reflection ablations, and a pen-spinning curriculum whose success requires pretraining plus fine-tuning.
Human rewards can initialize the loop; human text can replace reflection with one sample per iteration; 15 of 20 users prefer Eureka-HF despite lower reported forward velocity.
The prompt retains one reward/reflection pair; intermediate rewards use one PPO run, final rewards use five; headline normalized scores are clipped to [0,3] per task.
Experiments ran on eight A100 GPUs, each Eureka run took under one day, and the authors estimate four V100 GPUs with at most 8 GB per RL run can support the sixteen-candidate loop.
Dexterity aggregate statistics use 100 RL runs and 95% confidence intervals; Eureka training curves are less smooth than human-reward curves under PPO tuned for the latter.
The authors identify simulation scope, dependence on a human-definable fitness function, and evaluation on one fixed RL algorithm/simulator apart from limited exceptions as limitations.
The release loads prompts, extracts generated Python, injects it into task code and launches PPO subprocesses for candidates.
The release turns TensorBoard traces and errors into reflection, selects the maximum task score, keeps one reward/reflection pair in context and evaluates the best reward.
Pinned config defaults are gpt-4-0314, temperature 1.0, one iteration, three samples, 3000 PPO iterations and five final evaluations.
The README advertises sixteen samples and five iterations as defaults, conflicting with config.yaml at the same commit.
The release was tested on Ubuntu 20.04 and 22.04 and depends on NVIDIA Isaac Gym Preview 4 and an OpenAI API key.
Eureka was published at the Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024).
